cards.title: sshole

depth.text: someone found **locked accounts** on some Linux systems accepting **long passwords** as valid logins

On musl, `crypt()` **returns `*` for passwords over 256 bytes**, and OpenSSH can mistake that for the **`*` stored on a locked account**. After a wrong try, that account can accept passwords from **257 to 1024 characters**.

cards.camps: Some commenters fault musl's use of `*` as an error marker; others point to OpenSSH's handling of the hash and salt as part of the bug.

comments.text: OK, I think I see what’s going on with this, in this configuration. The goal from an attacker’s perspective is to get this to be true: `$ret = crypt($pw, $hash); $ret == $hash` when called by OpenSSH’s sshd. This is how sshd validates that the user logging in knew the account password. The `$hash` is the “settings” to the crypt call and will normally look like “$6$--gibberish” for users with…

My general rule of thumb is: "no magic strings". This is much easier to implement in higher-level languages and when writing application/web code than system programming. Don't return empty string/asterisk/anything else. Instead, return a failure value. When absolutely needed, choose the magic string with more caution: One string showing the SHA-256 of a non-existing hash? It's a good idea for it…

In-band signaling[1] strikes again. * should not have been used as special value, neither for "no password" in /etc/passwd nor "error while hashing the password" in crypt. I'm afraid we'll find many more of these abuses, specially in string manipulations. The null was ok, an exception (or equivalent) better, and Result<T> (or equivalent) best. [1]…

The whole story is a bit worse than this. Musl already worked around this type of failure . See the second-to-last line here: https://git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/crypt/crypt_des... (hey, this workaround is wrong if the salt is "x"!) but they forgot to work around it here: https://git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/crypt/crypt_sha... The vulnerable path in musl is only a little bit…

Above all, I’m a little sad that the musl developers decided to make a lot of “well it’s convenient” changes to core crypto functions — at least without the level of auditing that would have caught this! It’s tarnished their reputation in my eyes a little.

cards.title: Alpine Linux Security Advisory: OpenSSH-server password authentication bypass

depth.text: an **OpenSSH bug** lets attackers log in to Alpine machines **without knowing a password**

On affected Alpine setups, password logins must be on, and the machine needs an account whose password field is `*` plus another with a `$5$` or `$6$` hash. A password of **257 to 1024 bytes** can make passwordless accounts reachable in one connection; **fixed packages** are in Alpine 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say avoid Alpine or musl; others say static linking is worth it.

comments.text: musl’s crypt() returns the string * as an error indicator when the key is over 256 bytes long. * is also exactly what the stored field contains for every account with no password, so the “hash” matches and the login succeeds. Does anyone know why musl does this? Are they the only C library that behaves this way? For a C library that famously tries to adhere to POSIX as much as possible, this…

IMO this is where languages like Rust shine. The design patterns built into the language for handling errors (Result) - force you to handle errors / function results with sentinels, null pointers, or errnos are so much more error prone than handling a Result<T,E> using a match statement. crypt() returning `*` is insane especially since these kinds of sentinels are all over /etc/passwd
Discussion from a few hours ago: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50377221
I run Alpine on hardware. I was not effected by this as while I do use ssh keys, there are no user accounts without passwords on my server.
Given Alpine’s broad use in the Docker ecosystem, this is going to hit a lot of folks, I think.

cards.title: MCP Explained

depth.text: someone made a **guide** to how AI apps connect models with **tools and data**

**MCP** is an **open standard** for connecting AI apps to the tools and data they use. A server says what it can do, the app shows that to the model, then calls the server when the model wants something and hands the **result back**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say MCP is useful when deeply integrated into company platforms; others prefer command-line tools or ordinary APIs and say MCP adds little.

comments.text: This is too dense. You might as well just post some Python code with sufficient comments to get the same point across. I think a nicely written article with a few diagrams would go a long way. Sometimes less is more. MCPs don't really need this level of technical explanations (it's basically just a REST API with standardized endpoints for discovery aimed at agents), and AI agents really do lack…

Is it too much of an oversimplification to say "any new specialized tool or format that queries 'AI' with code is almost certainly pointless because you'll likely be able to match (and never exceed) that performance with an already known language, LLM query, or both?" Daniel Miessler's fabric comes to mind. It's great, does a lot of great stuff, but requires literally nothing new, "code-wise"

MCP is an enterprise tool. Anything fleeting -> just use a skill. The advantage of MCP is thin, and it only starts to show when it's really well integrated, and your company platform provider does the integration. Otherwise it's a huge pain in the rear to keep your cli integrated with all the MCPs. MCP is good for things you use literally 'all of the time' - or - it's seamlessly integrated into…
These vibe code explainers look nice on the surface but actually make things even more confusing. There's an element of curating which information to present and when that doesn't come across here.

Are MCP calls composable in e.g. codex yet? e.g. can a model pipe a jira MCP call to grep or sed, or at least into a file? Last I looked at MCP it was just a vastly worse version of curl, .netrc, and some short text files describing calls (which are themselves greppable). Is there anything useful beyond that that I'm missing?

cards.title: So my ISP was hijacking my DNS

depth.text: someone found their **ISP changing website addresses**, then learned what **encrypted lookups** can and can't protect

The first lookup returned an **IP owned by the ISP**, while Cloudflare's DoH endpoint returned a different one. The article explains that **DNSSEC checks responses** but doesn't encrypt queries; DoH and DoT encrypt traffic to the resolver, which you still have to trust. The author's setup uses **AdGuard with dnscrypt-proxy**, with Cloudflare as a fallback for some containers.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say ISPs may be required to alter DNS or that filtering can be fair; others see it as hostile meddling and ask why it isn't illegal.

comments.text: Noting this article skips over any discussion about why, or potentially (in the eyes of the law at least) legitimate reason an ISP might do this. Many ISPs in many countries are forced to do this for certain enforcement action that gets put upon them by their respective states for things such as age gating, censorship, monitoring, it varies state by state. And to be clear this is in no way an…

My workplace is messing with DNS as well, probably to filter specific websites, and I would not mind it since for the context of my usage that is perfectly fair. But their DNS responses have latency spikes every couple of minutes of 1-2 seconds that was driving me crazy. I simply enabled DNS over HTTPS in Firefox and everything feels so smooth now. I have no idea how my coworkers seem to be so…

I fear a future where pretty much everything is trying to hack you or doing something which is indistinguishable from the meddling of a hostile actor. I suppose the answer is politics rather than technology: Get enough people together to make a rule against it, and at least it will become niche.

Telecom Italia locks my DNS server (I cannot change it). I ended up using PIHole as DHCP, to drive home devices to PIHole, and control my privacy. The trick is simple: disable DHCP on your router, and activate it on PIHole.
As a bonus, PIHole on my RasperryPI2 is way faster than the little chip on my provider Router, and can be patched automatically with unattended upgrades.

cards.title: The lost malloc()

depth.text: someone dug through **old Unix code** and found **memory allocation ideas** we still argue about
Early `malloc()` and `mfree()` used **explicit memory regions**, and `mfree()` received the object's size. The author sees Unix's linear allocation and rollback as **close to arenas**.

cards.camps: Two camps: one commenter favors size-aware freeing so the allocator needn't keep a copy of the size; another isn't sold on arenas, saying they can waste memory and favoring a simple, flexible interface.

comments.text: The author did not really find from where SIMULA 67 had taken "new". In November 1965, C.A.R. Hoare published an extremely influential paper: "Record Handling". This was a proposed extension for the successor of ALGOL 60. Almost all of the features that were added in SIMULA 67 over its predecessor, the SIMULA language, come directly from the paper of Hoare, with two big exceptions: class…

> Not only that, mfree() receives the size of the object it is deallocating, as it should . I've always thought that one of the biggest tiny mistakes in the history of this industry. It means, more or less, that you're forcing the memory allocator to keep track of these sizes when it shouldn't have to. There's virtually no sensible case where the person calling free() doesn't know the size of the…

glossary.GrapheneOS: A privacy-focused version of Android, the software that runs many phones.
glossary.Android Open Source Project: The publicly available code that Android is built from, which developers can use to make their own versions.
glossary.hardened: Made tougher against attacks or unwanted access.
glossary.hardware blobs: Closed-source software supplied by a device maker to make parts of its hardware work.
glossary.awesome list: A community-made list of useful tools and resources for one topic.
glossary.pull request: A proposal to add your code changes to a shared project, usually asking others to review them first.
glossary.vibe-coded: Made by steering an AI with informal requests instead of writing most of the code by hand.
glossary.AI slop: Low-quality material produced quickly with AI, often in large amounts.
glossary.covert underperformance: Doing less useful work than the request calls for without telling the user.
glossary.CoT: Chain of thought: text showing an AI’s step-by-step reasoning while working on a task.
glossary.RL: Reinforcement Learning: a way to teach an AI by rewarding actions that get the desired result.
glossary.rubric: A set of rules for judging or scoring something.
glossary.yt-dlp: A tool for downloading videos from YouTube and other sites.
glossary.NAS: Network-attached storage: storage connected to your home network so other devices can reach its files.
glossary.Jellyfin: A way to organize and watch a personal collection of films and shows.
glossary.ytdl-sub: A helper for yt-dlp that automates video downloads and helps organize them by playlist.
glossary.Tdarr: A tool that automatically re-encodes video files, often to use less storage.
glossary.HEVC/H.265: A video format that can store video in less space, which can save disk storage.
glossary.MCP: Model Context Protocol: a standard way for AI apps to connect to outside tools.
glossary.JSON-RPC: JavaScript Object Notation Remote Procedure Call: a way for programs to send requests and replies to each other.
glossary.REST: A common way for one app to send requests to another app over a network.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.CLI: Command-Line Interface: a way to control a computer by typing commands instead of clicking buttons.
glossary.harness: The surrounding code that gives an AI agent tools and a place to work, and checks what it does.
glossary.machine learning: A way for computers to spot patterns in examples and use them to make guesses.
glossary.algorithm: A set of steps used to solve a problem or make a decision.
glossary.targeted advertising: Ads chosen using information about who someone is or what they do.
glossary.DNS: Domain Name System: the internet's address book, which helps a computer find a website from its name.
glossary.ISP: Internet Service Provider: a company that connects people to the internet.
glossary.IP address: A number that identifies a device or network on the internet.
glossary.resolver: A service that finds the internet address for a site name.
glossary.DNSSEC: Domain Name System Security Extensions: a way to check that lookup answers are genuine and haven't been changed.
glossary.DoH: DNS over HTTPS: a way to send website-name lookups through a protected web connection.
glossary.DoT: DNS over TLS: a way to protect website-name lookups as they travel over the internet.
glossary.DNSCrypt: A way to hide website-name lookups while they travel between your device and a lookup service.
glossary.PasswordAuthentication: An OpenSSH setting that controls whether people can sign in using a password.
glossary.AI accelerator card: A card built to handle the calculations used by AI programs.
glossary.memory bandwidth: How quickly a computer can move information in and out of memory.
glossary.inference: When an AI uses what it learned to answer or act, instead of being trained.
glossary.SRAM: Static Random-Access Memory: a kind of memory that keeps its contents while powered, so the computer can use them quickly.
glossary.HBM: High-bandwidth memory: fast memory placed close to a processor so it can get lots of information quickly.
glossary.TOPS: Trillions of Operations Per Second: a way to describe how many calculations a chip can do each second.
glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: the chip part that draws images and video.
glossary.retail park: A group of large shops outside a town centre, usually with parking nearby.
glossary.vacancy rate: The share of shops or other units that are empty.
glossary.footfall: How many people visit or pass through a shop or area.
glossary.business rates: A tax charged on business properties.
glossary.private equity: Investment firms that buy whole companies, try to make them earn more, then sell them.
glossary.base model: The starting AI that someone builds on or adapts for a particular use.
glossary.parameter: A setting inside an AI model that helps shape what it learns and produces.
glossary.token: A chunk of text an AI reads or writes, often a whole word or part of one.
glossary.fine-tuning: Training an already-built model a bit more on examples for a particular job.
glossary.context length: How much text a model can take into account at once.
glossary.pre-training: The first large training stage, where a model learns from its initial collection of examples.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.dependency: A piece of software a project relies on to do part of its job.
glossary.REPL: Read-Eval-Print Loop: a prompt where you enter a command and see the result right away.
glossary.open source: Software whose code is shared so other people can inspect, run, or change it.
glossary.residential proxy: A way to send internet traffic through a home or mobile internet connection, so it appears to come from that connection.
glossary.proxy SDK: Software Development Kit: a bundle of tools developers use to add features to an app; a proxy SDK can let a device's internet connection be used to send traffic.
glossary.Command and Control: A way for someone to send instructions to infected devices from afar.
glossary.exit node: A device that sends your internet traffic out to websites, which then see that device's connection.
glossary.JSON: A common format for storing and sending data in a way that programs can read.
glossary.streaming: Handling data as it arrives, rather than repeatedly asking for more.
glossary.UTF-8: A way to represent text so programs can read it consistently.
glossary.marshaling: Turning a Go value into JSON.
glossary.unmarshaling: Turning JSON back into a Go value.
glossary.open-weight: Describes an AI whose learned settings are available for others to download and use.
glossary.agentic coding: Having an AI handle coding tasks by making changes and checking its work with less step-by-step direction.
glossary.TerminalBench: A test that checks how well AI handles coding tasks through a computer’s text-based command line.
glossary.MoE: Mixture of Experts: a model with many specialist parts that sends each piece of text to only a few of them.
glossary.SFT: Supervised fine-tuning: training a model on examples of desired answers.
glossary.root access: Permission to control nearly everything on a device.
glossary.local privilege escalation: A way for someone already on a computer to gain more control, such as administrator access.
glossary.kernel: A small program that carries out a calculation on a computer's graphics chip or processor.
glossary.AI agent: An autonomous computer program that can carry out tasks.
glossary.agent orchestration: A way to coordinate several AI helpers so they can work on different parts of a job.
glossary.bead: A small work item given to an agent to tackle.
glossary.SVG: Scalable Vector Graphics: a picture format that stays sharp when resized.
glossary.raster-to-vector: Turning a picture made of pixels into one described with shapes and lines.
glossary.sprite sheet: A single image that packs multiple animation frames or game-art pieces together.
glossary.non-deterministic: Something that can give different results even when you use the same request again.
glossary.LED: Light-emitting diode: a small electronic light source used in bulbs and displays.
glossary.UV: Ultraviolet: a kind of sunlight that can harm skin.
glossary.incandescent: An older kind of bulb that makes light by heating a wire inside it.
glossary.compact fluorescent: A kind of bulb that makes light with a fluorescent tube.
glossary.PWM: Pulse-width modulation: a way to control power by switching a signal on and off in timed bursts.
glossary.IR: Infrared: light people cannot see, mentioned as another kind of light that bulbs may emit.
glossary.Code.Storage: A service the commenters describe as storing code and other files that change over time.
glossary.git: A tool that keeps a history of changes to code or other files.
glossary.diffs: A way to see what changed between two copies of a file.
glossary.OSS: Open-source software: software whose code is shared so others can inspect it and sometimes reuse it under a license.
glossary.agentic workloads: Computer tasks handled by AI agents rather than directly by a person.
glossary.foundation model: A model trained before use that can be adapted to handle different jobs.
glossary.single-cell representation: A computer-friendly description of an individual cell, used to work with or compare cell data.
glossary.physical field modeling: Using a computer model to work out how something physical, like heat, changes across space.
glossary.PacBench: A test used to compare how AI models do on the same game-building task.
glossary.cost/accuracy frontier: A comparison of which tools give the best results for their price.
glossary.post-training: Extra training after a model's initial training that shapes how it responds.
glossary.provable inference: A way to check that a response came from a particular model without running the model yourself.
glossary.zkSNARK: Zero-knowledge succinct argument of knowledge: a short proof that lets someone check a computation without revealing the model's hidden weights.
glossary.model commitment: A short fingerprint that pins down one exact set of model weights without showing the weights.
glossary.model weights: The learned settings inside an AI that shape how it responds.
glossary.mixture of experts: A way to build an AI from specialist parts, sending each question to the parts best suited to answer it.
glossary.formal verification: Checking a claim using precise rules, often with a computer.
glossary.microgravity: A condition where things seem almost weightless, often because they are falling together.
glossary.LEO: Low Earth orbit: a region fairly close to Earth where satellites travel around the planet.
glossary.sedimentation: Particles settling to the bottom of a liquid.
glossary.brain organoids: Small lab-grown groups of brain cells used to study how brain tissue behaves.
glossary.coding agents: Software that can take a request and carry out coding tasks, rather than just suggest text.
glossary.read-only: You can look at the information, but you can’t change it or add anything.
glossary.workspace: A saved work area that keeps a project’s files or conversations together.
glossary.moat: An advantage that makes it hard for competitors to take customers away from a business.
glossary.fork: A separate copy of a shared software project that people can take in a different direction.
glossary.reverse engineering: Figuring out how a program works by examining the program itself.
glossary.webhooks: A way for one service to automatically notify another when something happens.
glossary.VM: Virtual machine: a computer that runs inside another computer.
glossary.unikernels: A way to package an app with only the basic pieces it needs to run on a server.
glossary.LLMs: Large language models: computer programs trained on lots of writing that can produce text.
glossary.reversing: Tracing a program to figure out how it works, even without its original plans.
glossary.memory snapshot: A saved picture of the information a program is using at one moment.
glossary.trampoline: A small bit of code that briefly redirects a program somewhere, then sends it back.
glossary.WebRTC: Web Real-Time Communication: browser features for live audio and video calls.
glossary.DOSBox: A program that imitates an old DOS computer so DOS games can run on newer machines.
glossary.malloc(): A C function that asks for a block of memory while a program is running.
glossary.mfree(): An old Unix function for returning memory; callers gave it the size and which memory region to use.
glossary.linear allocation: A way of handing out memory by moving forward through one region, rather than finding separate free blocks.
glossary.arena: A reserved chunk of memory for related things that a program can keep around or clear as a group.
